No. Launching on 12 chains at once is usually a mistake for a new stablecoin, and "maximize reach" is the wrong goal at launch.

A stablecoin lives or dies on liquidity depth and trust in the peg. Spreading supply across 12 chains fragments liquidity into 12 thin pools, so each one has worse slippage, is easier to depeg locally, and is less attractive to market makers and integrators. One deep market beats twelve shallow ones.

It also multiplies your risk. Each chain means another deployment to audit, another set of admin keys and upgrade paths, and almost certainly bridges or a cross-chain messaging layer, which historically is where the largest exploits happen. A failure on any one chain hits the credibility of the whole asset. Operationally, you're also committing to 12 sets of monitoring, mint/redeem flows, compliance tooling (freezing and blacklisting have to work everywhere), and integrations with 12 different DeFi ecosystems.

Reach doesn't come from presence anyway; it comes from integrations: exchanges, lending markets, payment rails, wallets. Those partners care about liquidity and track record, which you build faster by concentrating.

The pattern that works for most issuers is to launch on one or two chains where your target users already are, get the peg, liquidity, and redemption process battle-tested, then expand using a native burn-and-mint setup (Circle's CCTP model) rather than wrapped bridge tokens. USDC and USDT both grew this way.

The exception is if you already have committed liquidity and integration partners on each of those 12 chains plus mature cross-chain infrastructure. If that's your situation, the calculus changes, but that's rare for a launch.
